expectedText:
CREDITOR'S CLAIM AGAINST A DECEDENT'S ESTATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan Rivera · Superior Court of California

PURPOSE OF THIS CREDITOR'S CLAIM INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet states general facts about the formal, statutory procedure set out at Probate Code § 9000 et seq. by which a creditor of Pat Morgan Rivera may file a claim against Pat Morgan Rivera's probate estate, now pending before Superior Court of California in Alameda County. It describes the claim-filing deadline, what a claim must contain, how and where a claim is filed, and what happens after a claim is filed or rejected. It does not itself file a claim on behalf of any creditor, does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes, and does not advise any specific creditor what to do about a specific debt.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "CLAIM," AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF NOT FILING ONE
Probate Code § 9000 defines a "claim" broadly to mean a demand for payment of a liability of Pat Morgan Rivera arising in contract, tort, or otherwise; a liability for taxes Pat Morgan Rivera incurred before death (other than property taxes and real-property-lien assessments); or a liability of the estate for Pat Morgan Rivera's funeral expenses — regardless of whether the demand is due, not due, accrued, not accrued, contingent, liquidated, or unliquidated. The same section defines a "creditor" simply as a person who may have a claim against estate property. Except as otherwise provided by statute, Probate Code § 9002 requires that all such claims be filed in the manner and within the time this part of the Probate Code provides, and states plainly that a claim not filed as this part provides is barred.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "“Claim” means a demand for payment for any of the following, whether due, not due, accrued or not accrued, or contingent, and whether liquidated or unliquidated: (1) Liability of the decedent, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise. (2) Liability for taxes incurred before the decedent’s death, whether assessed before or after the decedent’s death, other than property taxes and assessments secured by real property liens. (3) Liability of the estate for funeral expenses of the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9000(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9000(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9000.)
  "“Creditor” means a person who may have a claim against estate property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9000(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9000(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9000.)
  "(a) All claims shall be filed in the manner and within the time provided in this part. (b) A claim that is not filed as provided in this part is barred."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9002(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9002 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9002.)
  Known gap: The two § 9000 citations below (the definitions of "claim" and of "creditor") are both drawn from the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; the § 9002 citation is a separate, independently numbered section. This is California's own statutory definition and bar rule, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. Section 9000(b), not quoted here, separately clarifies that a "claim" does not include a dispute over title to specific property alleged to belong to the estate; that distinct carve-out is not addressed by this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether any specific demand qualifies as a "claim" or is barred — only a court, or the operation of the statute on a specific creditor's own facts, can do that.

THE CLAIM-FILING DEADLINE: THE LATER OF TWO DATES
Probate Code § 9100(a) requires a creditor to file a claim against Pat Morgan Rivera's estate before the later of two dates: four months after the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative, or 60 days after the date notice of administration is mailed or personally delivered to that particular creditor — whichever of the two comes later. The statute itself is explicit that this creditor-claim deadline does not extend the time provided by Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2, a separate, generally applicable one-year limitations period on actions against a decedent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) A creditor shall file a claim before expiration of the later of the following times: (1) Four months after the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative. (2) Sixty days after the date notice of administration is mailed or personally delivered to the creditor. Nothing in this paragraph extends the time provided in Section 366.2 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9100(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9100(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9100.)
  Known gap: This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 9100(a)); the two numbered deadlines within it are two ends of the same "later of" test, not independent provisions. Probate Code § 9103 separately allows a court, on petition, to permit a late claim in limited circumstances (for example, where the personal representative failed to give proper notice) — that late-claim petition procedure is a real exception to the deadline stated here but is not itself detailed in this clause. This clause does not independently verify the text or scope of Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 itself, which lies outside the Probate Code part researched for this document; it is mentioned only because § 9100(a) itself cross-references it. This is California's own statutory deadline, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims procedure — not a claim about which state's law, or which deadline, governs a specific creditor's specific claim.

WHAT A CLAIM MUST CONTAIN, AND HOW AND WHERE IT IS FILED
Probate Code § 9150 requires that a claim against Pat Morgan Rivera's estate be filed with the court — Superior Court of California in Alameda County, for a claim in this proceeding — and that a copy of the claim be served on Morgan Lee as personal representative, or on whoever is later appointed and qualifies as personal representative; a creditor who files with the court but never serves a copy on the personal representative (or vice versa) has an invalid claim. Probate Code § 9151(a) further requires that the claim be supported by an affidavit of the creditor, or of a person acting on the creditor's behalf, stating that the claim is a just claim, together with — if the claim is currently due — the facts supporting it, its amount, and confirmation that all payments and offsets have been credited, or — if the claim is not yet due, is contingent, or its amount is not yet ascertainable — the facts supporting it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) A claim may be filed by the creditor or a person acting on behalf of the creditor. (b) A claim shall be filed with the court and a copy shall be served on the personal representative, or on a person who is later appointed and qualified as personal representative. (c) Service of the claim on the personal representative shall be made within the later of 30 days of the filing of the claim or four months after letters issue to a personal representative with general powers. Service shall not be required after the claim has been allowed or rejected. (d) If the creditor does not file the claim with the court and serve the claim on the personal representative as provided in this section, the claim shall be invalid."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9150(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9150 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9150.)
  "(a) A claim shall be supported by the affidavit of the creditor or the person acting on behalf of the creditor stating: (1) The claim is a just claim. (2) If the claim is due, the facts supporting the claim, the amount of the claim, and that all payments on and offsets to the claim have been credited. (3) If the claim is not due or contingent, or the amount is not yet ascertainable, the facts supporting the claim. (4) If the affidavit is made by a person other than the creditor, the reason it is not made by the creditor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9151(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9151(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9151.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9150 and § 9151); neither is cited more than once in this clause. Probate Code § 9152, not addressed here, separately requires that a claim based on a written instrument attach the original or a copy of it, and § 9153 separately requires the Judicial Council claim form to include a proof-of-delivery section for the copy served on the personal representative. This clause does not address the additional service-timing rule in § 9150(c) (service on the personal representative generally due within the later of 30 days of filing or four months after letters issue) beyond what its quoted text below already shows. This is California's own statutory filing procedure, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law, or which court's local rules, governs a specific claim's filing.

THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE'S OPTIONS AFTER A CLAIM IS FILED
Once a claim is filed, Probate Code § 9250(a) requires Morgan Lee, as personal representative, to allow or reject the claim, in whole or in part; that allowance or rejection must be in writing, filed with the court clerk, and served on the creditor with a copy, and by statute must state (among other things) that the creditor has 90 days in which to act on a rejected claim. Probate Code § 9256 separately supplies a default rule for silence: if, within 30 days after a claim is filed, neither the personal representative nor the court has acted on it, the creditor may, at the creditor's own option, treat that inaction as equivalent to a notice of rejection given on the 30th day.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) When a claim is filed, the personal representative shall allow or reject the claim in whole or in part. (b) The allowance or rejection shall be in writing. The personal representative shall file the allowance or rejection with the court clerk and give notice to the creditor as provided in Part 2 (commencing with Section 1200) of Division 3, together with a copy of the allowance or rejection. (c) The allowance or rejection shall contain the following information: (1) The name of the creditor. (2) The total amount of the claim. (3) The date of issuance of letters. (4) The date of the decedent’s death. (5) The estimated value of the decedent’s estate. (6) The amount allowed or rejected by the personal representative. (7) Whether the personal representative is authorized to act under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (Part 6 (commencing with Section 10400)). (8) A statement that the creditor has 90 days in which to act on a rejected claim."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9250(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9250 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9250.)
  "If within 30 days after a claim is filed the personal representative or the court or judge has refused or neglected to act on the claim, the refusal or neglect may, at the option of the creditor, be deemed equivalent to giving a notice of rejection on the 30th day."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9256 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9256 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9256.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9250 and § 9256); neither is cited more than once in this clause. It does not address the separate procedure that applies when the personal representative is not authorized to act under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (§ 9251, court or judge review of the allowance) or when the personal representative or their attorney is personally the creditor (§ 9252). It also does not address § 9255's separate rule for a partial allowance the creditor refuses to accept. This is California's own statutory claims-response procedure, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate's claims administration.

THE CREDITOR'S DEADLINE TO SUE ON A REJECTED CLAIM
Probate Code § 9351 bars a creditor from suing Morgan Lee, as Pat Morgan Rivera's personal representative, on a cause of action against Pat Morgan Rivera unless a claim was first filed as this part of the Probate Code provides, and that claim was rejected, in whole or in part. Once a claim is rejected, Probate Code § 9353(a) bars the rejected part of the claim unless the creditor commences an action on it — or has the matter referred to a referee or to arbitration — within 90 days after the notice of rejection is given, if the claim was already due when rejected, or within 90 days after the claim becomes due, if it was not yet due when rejected. This 90-day claim-rejection deadline is a distinct, statute-specific time limit; it exists separately from, and operates in addition to, whatever generally applicable civil statute of limitations would otherwise apply to the underlying debt.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "An action may not be commenced against a decedent’s personal representative on a cause of action against the decedent unless a claim is first filed as provided in this part and the claim is rejected in whole or in part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9351 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9351 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9351.)
  "(a) Regardless of whether the statute of limitations otherwise applicable to a claim will expire before or after the following times, a claim rejected in whole or in part is barred as to the part rejected unless, within the following times, the creditor commences an action on the claim or the matter is referred to a referee or to arbitration: (1) If the claim is due at the time the notice of rejection is given, 90 days after the notice is given. (2) If the claim is not due at the time the notice of rejection is given, 90 days after the claim becomes due."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 9353(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 9353(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=9353.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9351 and § 9353); neither is cited more than once in this clause. It does not address § 9352, which separately tolls the otherwise-applicable statute of limitations on the claim from the time the claim (or a late-claim petition under § 9103) is filed through allowance, approval, or rejection, nor § 9353(b)'s separate rule excluding any period during which the personal representative's office is vacant. It also does not address the different procedure in Article 2 of this chapter (commencing with § 9370) that applies when an action or proceeding against the decedent was already pending at the time of death, rather than the no-pending-action situation addressed here. This is California's own statutory procedure and its own deadline, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law, or which limitations period, governs a specific creditor's specific claim.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet was reviewed on September 5, 2026, in Oakland, California. It states general facts about California's statutory creditor's-claim procedure in the administration of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate. It is not legal advice about any specific claim or debt, does not itself file, preserve, allow, or reject any claim, and does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes.
